source.title: Little Giants: Synthesizing High-Quality Embedding Data at Scale
source.authors: Hao-Nan Chen; Liang Wang; Nan Yang; Yutao Zhu; Ziliang Zhao; Fu-Ru Wei; Zhi-Cheng Dou

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends scaling analysis to synthetic-data training of text embedding models and reports MTEB performance as synthetic data size changes; it does not test language-model pretraining loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a synthetic-data-size scaling result for embedding-model benchmark performance. Its parameter, token, and compute counts are not varied to measure held-out language-model loss, and it does not test compute-optimal allocation. Other MTEB comparisons and alignment ablations are not results on the scaling relationship.
record.test_reason: The paper's own Section 4.4 result varies synthetic fine-tuning data size for a fixed 7B embedding model and reports how downstream MTEB score changes. That is a new setting (fine-tuning data for embeddings) with a downstream-performance scaling result. It bears loosely on V6 only: no held-out loss, parameters or compute are varied.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors report a log-linear relationship between embedding-model MTEB performance and synthetic data size. They say it lets one predict gains from more data and shows diminishing returns. Limitations states they did not fit a function and will explore a power law later. Note that Figure 4 nonetheless plots a 'Fitted Curve' whose form is unstated.
record.recipe_differences: Scales synthetic training-data size for a text embedding model and measures MTEB performance, rather than scaling language-model parameters, tokens, or compute and measuring held-out cross-entropy loss.
record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2024
record.problems: The scaling result is shown in a figure without numerical performance values or reported uncertainty. The authors state that they do not fit a function to the trend.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 2 report embedding benchmark comparisons and alignment ablations, not a controlled scaling relationship for this claim; not included.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss. Scaling of model parameters, pretraining tokens or compute. Any actual out-of-sample prediction: the authors only assert the trend enables prediction. Behaviour beyond about one order of magnitude of data.
Whether a power-law form holds in fine-tuning. The paper measures benchmark score, not loss. It does not fit a power law and explicitly defers that to future work.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small runs to larger ones.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Numeric anchor points on the scaling curve: 63.2 MTEB average at 230K synthetic samples and 63.4 at 920K. Also the y-axis range of about 62.6–63.4 across 100K–920K.
missing.locator: Table 2 (230K row), Table 1 (SPEED zero-shot row), Figure 4 axis

record.verdict_notes: The link to V6 is loose. 'Scale' here is fine-tuning (synthetic) data size for one fixed model, not model or pretraining scale, and the measure is benchmark score. The total effect is small: about 0.8 MTEB points over 100K–920K, with no error bars or seeds. A researcher may reasonably prefer to treat this as outside the claim. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute is not measured.
No small-run power-law fit is used to predict larger language-model runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal split is tested.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count are not tested.
The paper measures embedding benchmark performance against synthetic training-data size, not whether the same power-law form holds for held-out loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests MTEB performance against synthetic-data size for SPEED; does not test predictability from pretraining loss or model parameter/token/compute scaling.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups or fitting choices; no test of departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: Mistral-7B-v0.1
rows.stage_stated: embedding model fine-tuned using SPEED synthetic data
rows.operation_detail: Varies the size of the synthetic embedding training data and measures MTEB performance.
rows.measure: Embedding-model performance on MTEB as synthetic embedding data size increases
rows.note: The text explicitly describes a log-linear relationship between embedding-model performance and synthetic data size, and says the trend can predict improvements from synthesizing more data. The plotted performance values are not given numerically in the text. The authors state that they do not fit a function and plan to explore a power-law function in future work.
rows.check: Value is not fully unreadable. The figure's y-axis spans about 62.6–63.4 MTEB average. The text anchors two points: 63.2 at 230K (Table 2) and 63.4 at 920K (Table 1). The record should give these, roughly a 0.8-point gain over less than one decade (100K–920K). The figure legend shows a 'Fitted Curve', yet Limitations says no function was fitted. So the trend line's form and parameters are unreported.

relationships.condition: Mistral-7B embedding model fine-tuned on 100K–920K SPEED synthetic samples, MTEB zero-shot average
relationships.reason: r1: MTEB score rises roughly log-linearly with synthetic data size (about 62.6 to 63.4) with diminishing returns. The evidence is weak: under one decade, one model, no uncertainty, no numeric fit.
relationships.display_finding: MTEB increased roughly log-linearly from about 62.6 to 63.4 as synthetic data increased, with diminishing returns and no numerical fit.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
